public.prompt: Seven QuickRide delivery times are 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, and 80 minutes. The mean is about 30.9 min and the median is 22 min. Which measure best represents a typical delivery time for this batch, and why?

options.text: The median (22 min), because the single 80-min delivery pulls the mean well above where six of the seven orders actually sit.
The mean (30.9 min), because it uses every value in the calculation and is therefore the most complete measure.
The mode (22 min), because it is the most common value and therefore the most representative.
None of the above — you need to know the range before choosing a center measure.

opt_median.message: Correct. The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median. The 80-min outlier pulls the mean to 30.9 — nearly 9 min above where six of the seven orders sit — so the median (22 min) is the more representative typical value.

opt_mean.message: The mean does use every value, but that is exactly why it is misleading here. The single 80-min delivery pulls the mean to 30.9 min, well above the six orders that completed in 18–28 min. Using every value is not always an advantage when one value is extreme.

opt_mode.message: The mode names the most frequent value, but frequency alone does not make a value representative of the whole distribution. Here the mode and median happen to be the same (22 min), but the reason to prefer 22 min is that the median is robust to the extreme 80-min value — not that 22 appears twice.

opt_none.message: The range measures spread, not center. Knowing the range does not help you choose between mean, median, and mode. The choice depends on whether extreme values are present — and here the 80-min outlier makes the median the better center measure.

correct.message: Exactly right. When one value is unusually large, the median is more robust than the mean and gives a better picture of what is typical.

incorrect.message: Think about what happens to the mean when one value is much larger than the rest. Does 30.9 min feel like a typical delivery time when six of the seven orders finished in 18–28 min?

hints: Compare the mean (30.9 min) with the six orders that completed in 18–28 min. Does 30.9 feel like a typical delivery time for this batch?
The mean is computed by summing all values — including the 80-min outlier. The median is the middle value of the sorted list, so it is not pulled by extreme values.

import pandas as pd

median_val = df['delivery_time'].median()

public.prompt: The seven delivery times are 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, and 80 minutes. The range is 62 minutes. Which statement best explains the range's main limitation as a measure of spread?

options.text: The range uses only the two most extreme values and ignores how the remaining observations are distributed.
The range is expressed in squared units, making it hard to interpret directly.
The range does not use the mean, so it cannot describe how far observations sit from the center.
The range grows with sample size, so it is not comparable across datasets of different lengths.

opt_extremes.message: Correct. The range is max minus min, so it depends entirely on the two most extreme values. If all six non-outlier deliveries were exactly 22 min, the range would still be 62 min — even though the data would be far less scattered.

opt_units.message: Squared units are a limitation of variance, not the range. The range is expressed in the same units as the data (minutes here). The real problem is that it only looks at the two extremes and ignores everything in between.

opt_mean.message: Variance and standard deviation are the measures that use each observation's distance from the mean — not the range. The range's limitation is different: it ignores all observations except the largest and smallest.

opt_size.message: The range can grow with sample size, but that is not its main limitation. The core problem is that it is based only on the two most extreme values and tells you nothing about how the rest of the data are spread.

correct.message: Right. The range is max minus min — it only looks at the two extremes and ignores everything in between.

incorrect.message: Think about what the range formula actually uses: max minus min. How many of the seven delivery times does that formula actually look at?

hints: The range formula is: largest value minus smallest value. How many of the seven delivery times does that formula actually use?
Imagine replacing the five middle values (20, 22, 22, 26, 28) with a single value of 22. Would the range change?

solution_files.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('delivery_times.csv')

range_val = df['delivery_time'].max() - df['delivery_time'].min()
variance_val = df['delivery_time'].var()
std_val = df['delivery_time'].std()

print(range_val)
print(variance_val)
print(std_val)

tests.message_on_fail: range_val is not correct. The range is the largest value minus the smallest. Use df['delivery_time'].max() - df['delivery_time'].min().
variance_val is not correct. Use df['delivery_time'].var() — pandas divides by n − 1 by default, giving the sample variance.
std_val is not correct. Use df['delivery_time'].std() — it returns the square root of the sample variance.
The printed output does not match. Check that range_val, variance_val, and std_val are all computed correctly and printed in order.

correct.message: Well done. Range = 62 min, variance ≈ 481.1 min², std dev ≈ 21.9 min. The standard deviation tells you that a typical delivery time sits about 21.9 minutes from the mean — expressed in the original units, making it directly interpretable.

incorrect.message: Check each variable. Use .max() - .min() for the range, .var() for the sample variance (n − 1), and .std() for the standard deviation — all on df['delivery_time'].

hints: All three methods are called on df['delivery_time']: .max() - .min() for range, .var() for variance, .std() for standard deviation.
pandas .var() and .std() use ddof=1 by default, which means they divide by n − 1 — that is the sample variance and sample standard deviation.
